title: The Trap: Expecting a Self-Running Machine
The Real Model: You Are the Engine at First
Why It Has to Be Unscalable

html:
04 · Why it has to be unscalable

Scalable levers need a crowd. At the start, you are the only force.

“Scalable” tactics assume a force already in motion — word of mouth, a trusted brand. At zero users none exists, so disproportionate personal effort isn’t a compromise: it’s the only lever that connects.

02 · The trap

Expecting a self-running machine

Founders picture the finished company — users pouring in, systems humming — and assume the early days are a smaller version of that. But a running machine and a machine you're trying to start are two different situations.

03 · The real model

You are the engine at first

Early on, there is no momentum to coast on. The growth you see is the growth you personally create — through effort that could never work at large scale.

That's not a flaw in your plan. It's the whole job of the starting phase.

Like pushing a stalled car — it feels absurd to shove a machine meant to drive itself, but that shove is exactly what gets it rolling fast enough to start.
Fig. — Airbnb, New York: ~30 days going door-to-door

title: Cranking Is Also How You Learn

html:
01 · The core intuition

Startups don't just take off

The most natural assumption is the most misleading: that a good idea grows on its own. It won't. In the beginning nothing happens unless the founders make it happen — by hand, one push at a time.

Like a hand-cranked early car: the engine won't run until you physically turn the crank. Only once it catches does it drive itself.
Crank = founder effortCatch = self-sustaining growth
Instrument · cold startt = 0.0 s
Hold (or tap repeatedly) to turn it over. Let go before the catch point and it dies.

Crank 02 · Delight

Delight beyond what's reasonable

With a handful of users you can treat each one extraordinarily well. What should be insanely great isn't the product — it's the experience of being your user.

EXPERIENCE = PRODUCT + ATTENTIVENESS
Like a new restaurant where the owner personally greets every table — the food may be uneven, but the care makes people fall in love and come back.
Wufoo sent every new user a hand-written thank-you note. Tim Cook can't send you a note. You can.

title: The Idea Is a Vector, Not a Point

html:
Crank 04 · Concentrate the heat

Start narrow to catch fire

Manual effort only reaches so many people, so aim it at a deliberately tiny market you can fully dominate. Total saturation of a small space builds the density needed to spread.

Like a fire starting from a concentrated pile of kindling — spread the same flame across a whole field and it dies; pack it tight and it catches, then it can jump.
Case · FacebookLaunched Harvard-only: a potential market of only a few thousand — but a critical mass signed up because it felt made for them. It then stayed college-by-college for a while.

Crank 01 · Recruit

Recruit users one by one — the act is small, the compounding isn't

Don't broadcast and wait. Find individual people, reach them personally, set them up yourself. Each early user is won by hand, not attracted by gravity.

The hand-crank · Stripe's “Collison installation”

“We'll send you a link.”

One person, one setup, right now. That is the whole manual act — and it is what supplies the 10% you need each week. Drag the weeks →

Crank 03 · Learn

Cranking is also how you learn

The effort that grows the company and the effort that improves the product are the same effort — sitting with early users is the tightest feedback loop you will ever get.
One turn of the crank, two returns: users arrive, and they show you exactly what to fix.

11 / The reframe

The idea is a vector,
not a point

A startup isn't just what you'll build. It's what you'll build plus the unscalable things you'll do to get it started — a direction and a magnitude of effort.

That early hands-on push isn't scaffolding you throw away. Its habits — obsessing over users, learning by contact — often become the company's DNA, permanently.
